title: Project: Your Personal Brand Landing Page

scenes.narration: Welcome to Nabulines Academy. This is it — your first real project. Not a practice page. Not a demo. A landing page that represents you — your name, your work, your brand — that you'll actually share with people. By the end of this lesson, you'll have a live URL you can send to anyone. Let's build something you're proud of.

visual.title: Project: Your Personal Brand Landing Page
visual.subtitle: Ship something real

scenes.narration: What makes this a project and not just another lesson? Three things. First, you're making all the decisions — the design, the content, the vibe. I'm not giving you a template to fill in. Second, you're combining everything from Chapter Two — typography, color, layout, responsive design, images. And third, you're shipping it publicly. This page will be live on the internet with your name on it. That's the difference between practice and real work.

visual.title: What Makes This a Project
bullets: You make all the creative decisions
You combine every skill from Chapter 2
You ship it publicly — real URL, real audience

scenes.narration: Here's what your landing page needs. A clear headline that says who you are or what you do. A short bio — two or three sentences maximum. One high-quality photo of yourself or something that represents your work. Links to your socials or portfolio — GitHub, LinkedIn, Twitter, whatever you use. And a way to contact you — email, a contact form, or a call-to-action button. That's the minimum. You can add more, but don't skip these five.

visual.title: Required Elements
bullets: Headline — who you are / what you do
Short bio (2–3 sentences)
One strong photo
Links to your socials / portfolio
Contact method (email, form, or CTA)

scenes.narration: Design guidelines. Keep it simple — one or two sections maximum. Choose one accent color and stick to it. Use a single web font for headings and body text. Make sure it looks good on mobile first, then desktop. And use high-contrast text — dark on light or light on dark. No gray text on gray backgrounds. Readability beats style every time.

visual.title: Design Guidelines
bullets: Simple — one or two sections
One accent color, one font family
Mobile-first, then scale up
High contrast — readability first

scenes.narration: Let me show you how I'd start. I open Claude and say: Build me a personal landing page. My name is Alex Chen. I'm a designer learning to code. Use a clean layout with a hero section — my photo on the left, headline and bio on the right. Navy blue accent color. Links to GitHub and LinkedIn in the footer. Make it responsive. Claude generates the HTML and CSS. I see it in Artifacts. The layout is clean. The spacing feels right. But the photo placeholder is just a gray box, so I'll replace that with a real image URL. And I want the headline bigger — I tell Claude to make it sixty-four pixels on desktop. It updates instantly.

visual.caption: Building a landing page in Claude with real decisions

scenes.narration: Content tips. Your headline should be one clear sentence. Not clever. Not vague. Just honest. If you're a developer, say that. If you're learning to code, say that. Your bio is two sentences — what you do and what you care about. Don't write a resume. Write like you're introducing yourself at a meetup. For your photo, use something recent and high-resolution. If you don't want to show your face, use a logo or an image that represents your work. But make it sharp — no pixelated screenshots.

visual.title: Content Tips
bullets: Headline: one clear, honest sentence
Bio: two sentences — what you do, what you care about
Photo: recent, high-res, represents you
Links: only the ones you actually use

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. The first one is trying to say too much. You don't need five paragraphs about your journey. You need two sentences that tell people why they should care. The second mistake is bad contrast — light gray text on white, or dark blue on black. If you squint and can't read it, your visitors can't either. The third mistake is forgetting mobile. Half your visitors will see your page on a phone. If it doesn't work there, it doesn't work. And the fourth mistake is not shipping. Perfectionism kills projects. Your page doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to be live.

visual.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid
bullets: Saying too much — keep it short
Bad contrast — text must be readable
Ignoring mobile — test on a small screen
Not shipping — done beats perfect

scenes.narration: Once I'm happy with the design in Claude, I copy the HTML. I go to GitHub, create a new repo called landing-page, and paste the code into index dot html. I commit it. Then I go to Cloudflare Pages, connect the repo, and deploy. Two minutes later, I have a live URL. I open it on my phone to check the mobile layout. The text is readable. The image scales correctly. The links work. I copy the URL and paste it into my Twitter bio. That's it. The project is shipped.

visual.caption: Deploying to Cloudflare Pages and testing on mobile

scenes.narration: What to do after you ship. First, share the link. Post it on Twitter, LinkedIn, or wherever you hang out online. Say: I just built my first landing page. Here's the link. You'll get feedback. Some of it will be useful. Most of it won't. That's fine. The point is you shipped something real. Second, watch how people interact with it. Do they click your links? Do they reach out? If not, maybe your call-to-action isn't clear. Third, iterate. You don't have to rebuild the whole page. Just fix one thing. Make the headline clearer. Swap the photo. Adjust the colors. Small changes add up.

visual.title: After You Ship
bullets: Share the link publicly — get feedback
Watch how people interact with it
Iterate — fix one thing at a time
Keep it live — this is your brand now

scenes.narration: Ideas to level up your page. Add a custom domain — yourname dot com instead of a pages dot dev URL. We'll cover domains in Chapter Three. Add a dark mode toggle using CSS variables and a tiny bit of JavaScript. Add smooth scroll animations when elements come into view. Or add a contact form that sends you an email when someone fills it out. These are all small additions that make your page feel more polished. But don't add them now. Ship the simple version first. You can always improve it later.

visual.title: Ideas to Level Up (Later)
bullets: Custom domain (Chapter 3)
Dark mode toggle
Smooth scroll animations
Working contact form

scenes.narration: Here's why this project matters. You just proved to yourself that you can take an idea and turn it into something real on the internet. You didn't need a designer. You didn't need a developer. You didn't need a fancy tool. You used Claude, GitHub, and Cloudflare — all free — and you shipped a page that represents you. That's the whole point of this course. Not to memorize syntax. Not to pass a test. To build things and put them out into the world. This landing page is the first of many. Keep going.

visual.title: Why This Matters
bullets: You proved you can ship something real
You own this — it's live, it's yours
You didn't need anyone's permission
This is the first of many

scenes.narration: Your exercise: publish your personal landing page and post the link publicly. Share it on social media, send it to a friend, or just drop it in the course Discord. The goal isn't to get likes. The goal is to ship. Once you've done that, you're ready for Chapter Three — where we add custom domains, real interactivity, and start building apps that do things. See you there.
